utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, I was informed today that the Prosecution -- the Defence takes the position that it could cross-examine Mr. Cutler next Monday. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning. Thank you. Fifteen minutes ago, I was informed about the position of the Trial Chamber with regard to the examination of Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler. I have to say that I still haven't been handed the official translation of the supplementary information after the interview that was conducted with Mr. Cutler in the afternoon. I have to speak to General Galic and I believe that it will be on Monday that the cross-examination can take place of Mr. Cutler. Thank you for your understanding. I was told that it could be longer but due to continuity and the witnesses that are to follow, the Defence believes that it would be on Monday that the Defence would be able to cross-examine Mr. Cutler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you know, the Chamber would even have granted you a bit more time specifically because, as far as we can see, but of course the Chamber has not the full statement of Mr. Cutler that he gave before, but there seem to be new elements in this new information which might have asked for further investigation. So I see, for example, a Christmas party which would have taken place. But if the Defence is willing to consider to cross-examine Mr. Cutler by next Monday, the Chamber highly appreciates the flexibility and, at the same time, I would like to express that although the Prosecution might be under an obligation to inform the Defence, it is still a situation which could cause major difficulties in the progress of the trial. I have some understanding for the situation the Prosecution is in, but of course if you interview the witness during the last few days, then this kind of problems could arise easily. Similarly in respect of Witness AD, I am not going to say much about it, but from what we see now, it would have been perfectly possible, in my view, to at least indicate already to the Defence by mid-March that presumably there would be a request to put him on the list as well. As you know, this Chamber is very much concerned about proceeding as efficiently and as quickly as possible and if -- the Chamber is very grateful to the Defence that they show this flexibility at this very moment. Let's not spend too much time on it, unless there is a specific issue you would like to raise, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President, thank you very much. This issue has touched upon a procedure used by the Prosecution, and I think it appropriate and helpful if I might say a few words about that procedure because it may be that there are some misunderstandings at the moment. Firstly, my learned colleague has said that she has not yet received a formal translation. The fact of the matter is she received a draft translation yesterday and information sheets are only provided with a draft translation, not with a formal translation, because of the time that it takes to get a formal translation. Secondly, in relation to this particular supplemental information sheet, the first two paragraphs are within -- withdraw that -- repeat information which is in the statement already, with the exception, essentially, of six words which appear in the last four lines. So that passage is not new material, with the exception of six words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult for the Chamber to assess that because we only have the summary of the statements and not any further information. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I doubt that my learned colleague would dispute that. The rest of the supplemental information sheet content relates to issues which emerged for the first time to the knowledge of the Prosecution as well as to the knowledge of the Defence in the evidence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Henneberry. If I can emphasise that, the Prosecution had no forewarning that he would say what he did in relation to his conversations with Major Indjic and in relation to the briefings that he attended given by Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler and Mole. That being the case, clearly, it was relevant -- that led to relevant questions which you would expect us, Mr. President, to ask of Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler and Mole. That being the case, as a question of fairness, that should have been done in a proper form before the witness entered the box so that the Defence knew in advance, as much in advance as was possible in the circumstances, what his answers would be. So, Mr. President, in terms of procedure, it is my respectful submission that, contrary to the way it has been put to you by the Defence, this is in fact a proper procedure. As to the format of the supplemental information sheet itself, I made some enquiries before this trial commenced as to what procedure, if any, was followed by the Prosecution in earlier trials when information came to its attention immediately prior to the witness giving evidence or if there was relevant information available as a result of conversations with witnesses which wasn't in the form of a formal statement. Those enquiries revealed that, on occasions, that information was provided to the Defence, out of fairness. When it was provided, it was often done very informally. On occasions, the Prosecutor simply orally communicating it to the Defence perhaps minutes before the witness was called. I opted for this procedure that it be put in writing, that the Defence have the benefit of the name of the person who whom the information was conveyed, the date it was conveyed, and it be provided to the Defence in written form at the earliest opportunity. Therefore, the only issue really which arises here which in any way distinguishes it from the procedure which is applied with every witness in this trial, unbeknown to you, Mr. President, is the lateness of the information being provided, and I have explained why that is. If we had known months ago what Mr. Henneberry would have said, then, of course, those enquiries would have been made of Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler and Mole earlier than a matter of hours before Mr. Cutler was due to enter the witness box. Indeed, I was present during the proofing of Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler on the afternoon of Wednesday and Thursday, and I can assure you that it has been provided as soon as it could be provided. Mr. President, coming now to Witness AD, would it be appropriate to go into closed session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have to discuss it. If you say we can do it at a later stage -- it was just a small remark on the timing, but if you think that it is necessary to address the matter at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is not necessary at this very moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just establish -- well, perhaps the Chamber was most worried about, of course, the time the Defence had to prepare, and as I did indicate before, we have some understanding for the situation. On the other hand, we also have understanding for the Defence that needs time to prepare for cross-examination. We are not in a position to fully assess what is new, what is not new. But perhaps we established that the problem has been solved. You did not hear from the Chamber any criticism as to providing additional information sheets. That is not understood as to be improper procedure. You didn't hear me say anything like that. So perhaps we, if -- unless there is something that really needs either a decision or further consideration at this moment, I would just like to show that the Chamber is very glad that we could solve the problem, that it might be due to the flexibility of the Defence and with full understanding of the problems the Prosecution had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I come now for the proposed timetable for today. As I understand it, you have in mind that we do not call Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We were asked yesterday whether the examination-in-chief could take place today and then the Defence would still have time until next Monday to prepare for the cross-examination. That would mean that we start with Mr. Cutler, that if there is time left, that we will deal with available witnesses, and then start cross-examining Mr. Cutler by Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one remaining issue. I understand the course we will take today. In relation to Witness AD, there has been a document filed by the Defence. Do you wish a written response from the Prosecution or an oral response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider that and let you know. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to inform the Chamber that the Defence was not handed the translation of the supplementary information following the interview with Mr. Cutler. I would ask the Prosecution to hand it over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was sent by fax yesterday. It may have gone to -- I wonder whether in fact it has gone to the fax number for Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It was sent at 6.00 p.m. -- excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It was sent to a number in The Hague which has been provided to us by the Defence, but in any event, I appreciate my friend doesn't have it and we will provide a copy during the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you will provide it to her, and apart from that, you will check your fax and phone numbers. This technical communication will not cause us any problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I be excused, Mr. President? Mr. Mundis will take Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, just for the understanding for the Chamber, the information I just mentioned about your willingness to cross-examine the witness on Monday and your willingness to agree to start the examination-in-chief by today, that is correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I informed the Chamber and I proposed that we would be able to hear the examination-in-chief of Mr. Cutler and then the Defence would start with the cross-examination on Monday, but, of course, it will be good for me to get a hold of this translation. I did not get it by fax. There would be no reason for me to say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a copy here, together with our fax report, that it was sent to a particular number and the result was that it was sent. But I have a copy for my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you tried to send it and Ms. Pilipovic did not receive it. Mr. Usher, could you please pass the copy of the Prosecution to Ms. Pilipovic. Would you have two copies so that General Galic could also have one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At this stage, Mr. President, I only have the one. But I will provide a second copy at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So the order for today has been fixed. Mr. Mundis, would you please call your next witness, Mr. Cutler, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the fact that my learned colleague has just been handed the draft translation, if she needs a brief recess, we are certainly happy to allow that to happen before I call Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you would need more time at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that perhaps if we have a break at half past 10.00, I would be able to inform General Galic about the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that would be sufficient to you. Then, Mr. Mundis, please call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution calls James Cutler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Cutler into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cutler, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cutler, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cutler. Please be seated. Mr. Cutler, counsel for the Prosecution is the first to examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I am Mr. but ex -- retired Lieutenant-Colonel James Philipe Cutler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler, can you tell us what military you are retired from?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I am retired from the New Zealand Army and I was an officer in the Royal New Zealand Regiment for 32 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the course of your military career, were you posted at any time to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I arrived from New Zealand on the 29th of November and was posted -- I flew into Sarajevo as a senior military observer on the 21st of December, 1992, and officially took over from Lieutenant-Colonel Richard Mole on the day after Christmas, [Realtime transcript read in error " "] the 26th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As senior military observer, can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what your duties and responsibilities consisted of?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: The tasks of the UNMOs under my command, which numbered about 60, was to monitor the airport agreement, to monitor the heavy weapons concentration sites, to monitor prisoner of war and body exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. In the transcript, there is no date, the 26th of December, when Mr. Cutler started his duty. I believe that is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is my recollection that the witness testified that he took over from Mr. Mole on the 26th of December, and we only see the 21st of December as the date of your arrival in Sarajevo. So that has been corrected for the transcript now. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have covered the -- to monitor the airport agreement, to monitor the heavy weapons concentration sites on both sides, to monitor prisoner of war and body exchanges, to monitor the incoming and outgoing fire on both sides, and from the main mandate, to provide our best humanitarian efforts anywhere we could and to generally report the situation as it was reported by UNMOs so that those reports would go through to high headquarters. Those were the major tasks. I added a final task of trying to spread the word on both sides as to what all the UN agencies in Sarajevo were trying to achieve. That would be about the major tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did your assignment in Sarajevo come to a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I packed by bags and had a farewell party on the night of the 14th of March, 1993, and flew out on the 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have testified that you had approximately 60 UNMOs under your command. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how those forces were distributed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I had a small headquarters at the PTT building in Sarajevo. It varied between 8 and 10 people. There was myself, a DSMO who, during my time, I had two captains from Canada: James de Rosenroll, followed later - and he was with me most of the time - Major Kent Carswell. I had a utilities UNMO, and at my time there, a very brave lad, name of Flight Lieutenant Jim Finlayson. He was in charge of utilities missions. I had other UNMOs involved with utilities missions. There was one in particular I remember. I had double heading of UNMOs in that headquarters, transport logistics looking after generators ration --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Everything has to be translated both in Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian and in French. So the interpreters need some time to follow your words. Please proceed. To my surprise, I get the French translation on the English channel at this very moment - perfectly translated, I admit - but perhaps for those who are dependent on the English text, the translation was just what I said. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, you mentioned a DSMO. Can you tell us exactly what that acronym stands for?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. That is the deputy senior military observer. So that if I was absent, away on leave or not in the headquarters, he would deputise as the SMO. So I had my small headquarters within the PTT, that was co-located with Sector Sarajevo, who was commanded -- which was commanded at that time by Colonel Razek, and later a very fine French gentleman by the name of Colonel Valentin. So that was my headquarters. On the Papa side, on the Presidency side within Sarajevo, I had three major observation posts and one Papa headquarters. The Papa headquarters, which consisted of about three or four UNMOs, was located adjacent to the Presidency in the centre of town. I had three major observation posts going from west, around from east to west, Papa 6, which is on the south-eastern flank of Sarajevo; Papa 4 was on the central north of Sarajevo; and Papa 5, to me the most strategically important observation post, was north-west, overlooking the whole basin of the airport, Otes, Stup, Rajlovac, and those sorts of areas. And we could see that particular OP directly from -- from the PTT. I just had to go out on my landing and could see it over the hill. On the Bosnian Serb side, the number of OPs varied, but when I got there, I think it was 7 or 8. We had a -- what we called the Lima headquarters which was co-located with the 1st Corps Sarajevo Corps. That was a small headquarters of about three or four UNMOs. Whilst I was there, a New Zealander had just left, Commander Gwyn Rees, as the subsector commander. Commandant Michael Beary took over from him. I then appointed a Captain Pat Henneberry to take over from him, and under their control were these seven OPs on the Bosnian Serb side. They basically surrounded Sarajevo from Lima 7 on the extreme eastern flank coming around both sides. I don't think I need to go into the detail of their exact locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, you referred to the 1st Corps Sarajevo Corps. Which military corps was that a component of?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I understood it to be the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the Lima headquarters was co-located with the 1st Corps Sarajevo Corps. Where was that physically located, the Lima headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: It was located on the western end, on the ground floor of that building, going the entrance way to the left and down the corridor, and they were on the extreme left. They had a fairly cramped, what I will call their main operations room, and through the -- to the end of the building was their sleeping accommodation. I think there was one other room they used there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This building was located in the Lukavica barracks compound?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the reporting mechanisms that were in place during the period you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Purely on the UNMO, the United Nations military observer, the reporting was on a daily basis, every day, of what had occurred in the previous 24 hours. That reporting followed a fairly set sequence and ended with the number of incoming and outgoing rounds for any particular day. The report would normally start with the general situation, whether it was a low intense day, a tense day, or a day of high activity. It would then detail the main areas where shelling had occurred and any other activity or front line activity was reported as best the UNMOs could. I say, "as best they could" because to do the job really efficiently, we would have needed another 200 UNMOs to really cover the ground. But they reported the best they could. These reports also included a lot of administrative matters as part of that daily sit-rep. These sit-reps would be compiled at the subsector headquarters on the Lima site and the Papa side and then forwarded by 8.00 every night to my headquarters in Sarajevo. I would then, and my staff, would analyse those and compile the daily sit-rep for UNMOs Sarajevo and they would then be sent off to the sector, copies to the Chief Military Observer in Kiseljak, who was responsible for UNMOs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the exception of Sarajevo because my reporting line was direct to the Chief Military Observer located in Zagreb. Copies of our sit-reps went to all of these people. Of course, the Sector Sarajevo and the Colonel Razek and Colonel Valentin would also produce their sit-reps. They would quite often take the activity of the day out of our main sitrep and include it in theirs. So there was quite often double reporting going up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there also monthly compilations of the sit-reps that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of -- the week after the end after each month, a monthly, full monthly report would be compiled and that would have been compiled from the main activities that had occurred from all sit-reps. In other words, it would be a paraphrasing of the sit-reps for that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you also prepare any type of written reports for the New Zealand government?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. My directive appointing me as the senior New Zealand National Officer, specified that I was to send a report in the form of a situation report back to New Zealand, two of them within the first week and from there on as I saw fit. But I interpreted that as a -- tried to get one at least one a week. I had nine New Zealand UNMOs under my national command that was spread all over Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and some in Sarajevo. I had that responsibility to make sure that their -- of their welfare and I was required to report back to New Zealand. Those reports would consist of listing of all air UNMOs, where they were, how they were, if they were still smiling or if they weren't happy. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Administrative matters took up quite a bit of time, and also how I perceived the situation within Bosnia-Herzegovina and, in particular, Sarajevo where I was posted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the context of these reports to New Zealand, when you say, "our UNMOs," you are referring to New Zealand UNMOs --

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- posted in the region. During the course of your tenure in Sarajevo, did you on any occasion have the opportunity to meet with any Bosnian Serb military officers?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. From the day I arrived in Sarajevo, I was immediately sent out to go and meet the UNMOs in the various sites. I visited the Bosnian Serb side from first going into Lukavica headquarters; I think it was the 22nd. I was over there for two days. I only recall meeting one or two Serb commanders. At that time, I went around all or most of the OPs on the Lima side. I met various commanders on that first trip, the same on -- then I came back into the PTT and did the Papa side. It was a pretty quick introduction but I must say a very valuable introduction. There had been certain things occurring which I was disturbed about and it was obvious that and Richard Mole's -- Colonel Richard Mole's handover to me, I realised I had to go and meet the corps commander on the Bosnian Serb side, and hopefully his staff, to introduce myself and to start talking about the things that were of major concern in Sarajevo. So I wrote a letter to General Galic, whom I understood had just been promoted to general, basically saying, "I am the new SMO, very glad to be here, look forward to a good working relationship with you," and asked him if I could come over and visit, and that was about another two days' time. As a result of that, I got approval to do that, went across to the Lukavica headquarters. For some reason, there had been a delay, the meeting was turned off, but I did meet General Galic as he was going out of his headquarters with a group of other officers. We shook hands, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date that you met General Galic as he was exiting his headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: It was probably either very late December or early, very early January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: December 1992, January 1993?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity in early January 1993 to meet with any other senior members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. As a result of the letter, I got a meeting, but it was not with the corps commander, but it was, as I understood at the time, the Chief of Staff, which I was delighted with, Colonel Marcetic. I have difficulty in pronouncing that word but it was "Marcetic." We had a meeting on the floor above the ground floor, which was the first floor, in a room -- quite a large room with a large conference table in it. Present were myself, the interpreter at that headquarters, I think it was Captain Pat Henneberry. There was also Colonel Marcetic, and there one or two other Serb officers there, and I do not recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, you've mentioned that this was in a room above the ground floor. Would this be in the Lukavica barracks headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if Colonel Marcetic, in addition to being the chief of staff, do you recall if he was introduced to you in any other terms or with any other title?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: No, but I had -- later on, I received a letter signed by him in relation to suspected artillery and mortar positions on Mount Igman and he signed himself off as the deputy corps commander. He may have been promoted or I don't know but he was -- we had him first of all as Chief of Staff. Later on, he was obviously the deputy commander because that is what he signed himself as.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you subsequently have additional meetings with Colonel Marcetic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that first meeting at which I discussed the problems confronting us at the time, and I had several other formal meetings with him. And there were one or two also informal meetings if I happened to be in the headquarters and he would be there, and it would be almost fleeting but I would get a few words in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall during your tenure in Sarajevo approximately how many times you met with Colonel Marcetic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: It would be in the order of 6, 7 or 8 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you had any meetings or introductions to anyone who was introduced to you as the Bosnian Serb army liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that occurred on my initial visit. It was pointed out to me that the office directly across the corridor, it was a 6 foot wide corridor, that is where the Serb LO was. I understood his name to be "Jakavic" because that is what I have written in my diaries. His name could have been "Indjic" but I regarded Indjic as being the Serb LO in the PTT. I may have got those two names mixed up, Jakavic and Indjic. I met him on several occasions. I didn't speak to him a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me attempt to clarify. Based on your previous answer, is it correct that there were Bosnian Serb army liaison officers in both the PTT building and the Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in one of those locations was a person by the name of Indjic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I understood him to be in the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And there was another Serb liaison officer at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Correct. And I understood him to be Jakavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: A person --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please make a pause between the questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The person whom you believed to be Jakavic, do you recall approximately how many meetings you had with him?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: He was the liaison officer with the corps headquarters, the Bosnian Serb Corps headquarters, with my UNMOs. I had a great deal to do with him, obviously. I -- really, my conversations with him would not have been lengthy. They would really just have been: "Hello, how are you," et cetera. I didn't have any detailed meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The person whom you have described as Indjic, approximately how many meetings did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I didn't have many meetings with him at all, but I saw him on many many, occasions, particularly when shelling was occurring within Sarajevo, which was suspected to be coming from the Bosnian Serb side. Either I or one of my UNMOs would be downstairs. We were on the fourth floor of the PTT. We would be downstairs very quickly and saying, "Can you see if you can get Lukavica to stop this firing?" There was one particular occasion which relates to Papa 5 in which Papa 5 was being, I believe, deliberately shelled - in fact, on more than one occasion - that I raced down myself and forgot to open the door handle, and it was a glass door and I went right through the door. That is how angry I was at that particular time. But I saw him on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will deal with specific instances where you met with these individuals in a few moments. Let me ask you if you were aware of the ranks of these two individuals, these two liaison officers, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I seem to recall that Indjic in the PTT was a Major. That was my perception. I seem to recall that Jakavic may have been a major when I arrived, but may have been promoted whilst I was there. That was the impression I got. I have no proof of that, but that was my perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return to your arrival and your handover from Lieutenant-Colonel Mole. Can you briefly describe for us the general situation as reported to you by Lieutenant-Colonel Mole at the time you assumed command?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Just prior to me arriving in Sarajevo, there was what Colonel Mole described the battle of Otes, which was on the western flank of Sarajevo city. There had been intense battle, preceded by heavy artillery concentrations, tank fire, anti-aircraft fire, and very intense front line infantry attacks. The front lines in that particular area were very close. Colonel Mole told me that I had arrived at a good time because they were licking their wounds and removing bodies from the battle site. And a total evidence would indicate there was many casualties on both sides, and once again, anecdotal evidence would indicate it was a time when the Bosnian Serb Army, the Sarajevo Corps, realised that there was some very strong resistance, and I think there was a lot of loss of life on the front lines on both sides. That was the general situation militarily, but also there were other concerns like shelling of Kosevo hospital, what was described as indiscriminate shelling throughout the city, which was continuing to keep the population or the morale of the population at a low ebb. That was generally the situation in relation to UNMOs. It disturbed me greatly that it would appear that both sides had great delight on sniping of UNMO vehicles, on UNMO OPs, and also there had been the odd close shelling to UNMO OPs within Sarajevo. That, as I recall it, was the situation when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Within the first week to 10 days that you were in Sarajevo, you have testified that you got out to the various Papa and Lima OPs. Did you gather first-hand information from your UNMOs on both sides of the confrontation line as to the situation upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I have to admit that the information I received from various sites in some cases was conflicting. There was certainly no peace in Sarajevo, that there was a war in Sarajevo or that a -- Sarajevo was under siege, there is no question about that in my mind. The population was not free to come and go as they pleased. Winter was approaching. UNHCR were having difficulties getting the quantities of food. UNHCR, I presume is a common term, were having difficulty getting the quantities of food in. There had been no water or electricity for quite some time. And things in the city were quite grim. The -- as to the UNMOs and the OPs, as a professional officer, not at all satisfied with some of the construction of the OPs. Sandbagged roofs were about to collapse. In Papa 4, the ceiling was about to collapse. There were too many sandbags on top of. So I had all these internal matters to consider as well, and make arrangements for -- through Colonel Razek with engineers from the Egyptian Battalion to start assisting to make life a bit more safe for the UNMOs in their OPs, particularly within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, you mentioned that things in the city were quite grim. Do you recall sending a sit-rep back to the New Zealand authorities on 2 January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I sent a sit-rep back about that time. If it was 2 January, I will accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall in that sit-rep providing information about life in Sarajevo for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that well. It -- for a person from New Zealand to see what I saw in Sarajevo was not very nice. And the total evidence from talking to UNHCR people was that this was their second winter, they were approaching their second winter. They were concerned about the state of the hospitals, lack of medical supplies, firing on those hospitals. Doctors had been killed, patients had been killed. I was struck by watching very proud people walking through the streets. Normally, the children would run between containers that were put up to stop the sniping from the southern side of the main river that runs through Sarajevo. Most people would run between those barriers. The -- I was struck by the -- how well dressed the young ladies were and how proud they seemed to be, going about their, as well as they could, their daily business. Children were very well dressed and playing in the streets. But there were others that you would wonder why -- a 6 foot gap between containers, more elderly people would walk between them with their heads held high and not worry about being shot at. We couldn't quite understand that. I interpreted a lot of these things as being defiance and "I don't care if I get killed." I heard stories of little old ladies living on their own on the corner of the street who, when they were delivered food, basically said, "I don't want any food. I don't know if I will make it through this winter." It was -- it was a sad situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall again in early January 1993 reporting back to the New Zealand authorities the following: "As soon as the command 1st Sarajevo Corps Serb side is back in his office, I have the task of trying to convince him that the shelling of hospitals and grave sites is really not on"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I remember that extremely well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were you referring to when you made this report back to Wellington?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I was referring to many reports that I had received about shelling in and around Kosevo hospital and also reports that funerals that were being conducted had been fired on, the Kosevo hospital and the funeral site graveyard not being that far apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During your tenure in Sarajevo, do you recall approximately how many reports you received about shelling at Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I received several formal written reports and, in particular, a witness report of shelling on the hospital, early January, about the 11th of January, I think it was, and further reports towards the end of January, 29th and 30th of January, which were most disturbing. They were formal reports I received, but there were also other reports during the month of January that we got that there was shelling of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were in Sarajevo, did you cause any investigations to be carried out with respect to shelling of Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I didn't cause any investigations to be carried out because that was really the job of the subsector Papa UNMO, Lieutenant-Colonel Carl Harding and his team. There was an investigation that he kicked off, initiated, after the shelling on the 29th and 30th of January. It was conducted by a Major Vislov and a Captain Baker, and I think those reports are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I ask that the witness be shown the document marked P745.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, it is on your list that we are dealing with, mainly Rule 70 documents, so could you please keep that in mind. So we will not put them on the ELMO and I don't know whether any of the information from these documents needs protection as well, then you indicate it, and then we will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will do so, Mr. President. I am intending, just for the benefit of the Chamber and the Defence, to simply have the witness identify the documents and they will be then subsequently tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, I see you have before you P745. Without describing the contents of this document, can you verify that this document refers to the investigation you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document consists of a cover page that you created and signed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And two subsequent statements of individuals who investigated the shells of Kosevo hospital in late January 1993?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That document can be retrieved from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, during the course of your tenure in Sarajevo, do you -- or did you receive any information that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was using the hospital grounds to launch mortars?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, there had been a lot of rumours floating around that, in fact, mortars were being used or various United Nations installations, the locations of the Egyptian and Ukrainian battalion, and in particular, the Kosevo hospital had been used to screen firing of mortars by the Presidency forces. On the -- I was obviously delighted that on the second week in January, I think it was on the 12th of January, a colonel sergeant from the British Cheshire regiment, who had been in charge of mortars, asked to see me. He had been asking who he could give a statement to. I welcomed him into my office and I took a statement from him that involved him witnessing the fire of a mortar, an 82-millimetre mortar, from adjacent to the Kosevo hospital. I think it was early afternoon. The Colonel sergeant had been escorting a convoy of fuel to that hospital. He and his crew observed this mortar firing five rounds from the hospital, adjacent to the hospital grounds, as part of the hospital grounds. The mortar then stopped firing. The colonel sergeant questioned one of the hospital administrators as to, "Does this happen very often?" And the administrator said, "I am not military. There is nothing I can do about this." On leaving the hospital grounds, which would have been in the order of 30 minutes later, the hospital came under mortar, artillery, and anti-aircraft fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, you testified at page 25, line 24, that you were obviously delighted about this development. Can you elaborate or explain why you were delighted that this report came across your desk?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: As I think I wrote in my covering letter to General Morillon, we had been -- suspected that mortars were using hospitals and UN installations from which to fire their weapons. I had been told in previous meetings by Colonel Marcetic that they suspected that mortars were firing from the hospital location, and this was the first real eyewitness proof that we had that indeed that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience in Sarajevo in late December and early January 1993, late December 1992, early January 1993, were you able to draw any generalisations about the patterns of incidents where the city of Sarajevo received incoming artillery or mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: The pattern to me was there were two distinct patterns. There was obvious front line firing. This is both sides firing on the front lines, I assume into the trenches. Pure military activity to either on the Presidency side to gain ground at the mortars preceded by or -- infantry probes preceded by mortars and artillery, and the same on the Bosnian Serb side. Then there was shelling. That was the pure military side, as I call it. Then there is the other side which I would call "harassing fire" into the city, and it was no particular place. It seemed to be all over the city. From a professional point of view, I could understand that there would be various targets throughout Sarajevo, not necessarily military. But to me there were two distinct phases: Front line activity and harassing indiscriminate within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the second component, this indiscriminate and harassing firing within Sarajevo, as you have described it, did that seem to follow any certain type of pattern that you were able to discern?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I always listened carefully to what Colonel Marcetic had to say. And also at later meetings that I attended with General Morillon, with General Mladic, General Gvero, that the Bosnian Serbs would only fire in retaliation to outgoing Bosnian fire. This indeed, as a generalisation, seemed to be the case. In the February-March period, that was -- seemed to be particularly evident to the stage where we would get up in the morning, 6.00, no activity whatsoever and then we would hear a couple of "pop pops" which were obviously outgoing mortar fire from the Bosnian, and within a short few minutes later, there would be incoming fire, and normally the incoming fire would be more than two rounds. If two rounds were fired out, it would be something in the order of 10 to 15 rounds would be incoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you briefly to clarify something. On page 27, line 25, you said, "Obviously outgoing mortar fire from the Serbs and within a short few minutes later there would be incoming fire."

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I apologise. From the Bosnian Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you would hear outgoing fire from the Presidency side, the Bosnian side, followed by incoming?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. There was a very interesting situation developed which I hadn't realised, that there was no outgoing fire for several days. The pattern was in troughs and peaks of the shelling. And several days we would have no firing. When I say, "no firing" I would mean low activity. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There would also be some form of front line activity, small arms, the occasional mortar going off, but we regarded that as very low level activity. But some days, the UNMO's OPs would not report any outgoing, and in the PTT we would not hear any outgoing and yet we would hear explosions going off in the distance. Once again, Colonel Marcetic alerted me to the fact that incoming fire onto the Serbian side, particularly Ilidza, was coming from Mount Igman. Indeed, towards the end of my tour after I had many or had a lot of meetings with Colonel Marcetic, and after one particular meeting which we will probably go on to later, he was good enough to ring me up, to contact me via his liaison officer through my UNMO headquarters in Lukavica, to tell me or to warn me to "Tell the Bosnians to stop firing on Ilidza or we will hit Sarajevo." By that I meant, I interpreted, because there was no outgoing fire from the Presidency side, that Ilidza was being hit and indeed we could hear that. And it was, according to the Serb headquarters, was coming from Mount Igman. There was not a great deal we could do about it except to tell the Bosnian allies to, "Tell your people to stop firing." That didn't occur, and as a result Sarajevo was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have testified about the shelling incidents coming in peaks and troughs. Were you also aware of sniper activity in the month of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: That was best described as an occupational hazard. There was sniping; it was continuous and frequent, nearly every day. Some days would be much more intense than others. I don't think there was an UNMO vehicle, any vehicle for that matter, convoys, that was not fired upon. It was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience in Sarajevo, did the sniping activity similarly follow peaks and troughs?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to the middle of January 1993. Do you recall any information or reports coming to you with respect to the Serbian New Year?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I made a what could be regarded as a throw away or frivolous comment in a situation report that we expected fireworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why was that the case?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Because we knew that the Serbian New Year was about to be celebrated. I had been educated in the different dates from what I am used to, 25 December and 1 January, there is a 7 January, 12, 13 January. And I had been at the Serbian Christmas dinner in Pale and I knew a week later that it was going to be their New Year. And so I wrote that comment in that sit-rep and, sure enough, we got fireworks display which consisted mainly of anti-aircraft fire from where I was standing, from my left, which was south in the vicinity of over the back of a feature called Mojmilo and around to Lukavica, firing over into what is known as the feature Zuc. And it was tracer, red tracer, which they -- the tracer bullets would send red lights as they travelled through the air. And there was generally a, what one could term a "yippie."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: A "yippie"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: A "yippie," a shoot-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know or did you witness any type of increase in shelling or mortar activity during the Serbian New Year 1993?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, there was an increase, but it was relatively short-lived. There was anecdotal evidence, which I have absolutely no proof for, that perhaps some of the Serb gunners had had too much to drink and may have just gone outside and decided to celebrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were touring, for lack of a better word, the Lima side, at any time during your tenure, did you have the opportunity to visit any Bosnian Serb army artillery or mortar positions around the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I visited mostly heavy weapons concentration sites just to get a feel for what was going on. I didn't stay there long. The sites I recall were on the -- up through Pale. I think it was Lima 7 that had an absolute glorious view of Sarajevo, and there was a lot of fire power on that side. I stood on top of where the Lima 7 UNMOs would do most of their observation from, and looking down to my left, there were batteries scattered around the slightly lower ground. I went to a place on -- around the opposite side where the weapons were described to me as a mortar family, started off as a very large mortar, coming right down to a 60-millimetre mortar, that were all lined up. They called it "the mortar family" for obvious reasons. And I visited a gun line not far from the Lukavica headquarters, that would have been further to the south, where the commander on my request asked me if I would like to go and have a look at the guns. And I did so. There was only one or two Serb gunners walking around at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the gun site that you visited in terms of its fortifications?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I did not -- by "fortifications," do you mean pits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Pits, or if the guns were dug in or sandbagged or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: No, there was very little protection in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing similar protection in other locations?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: From a distance, and we are talking about a thousand metres, and looking through on the eastern side, there seemed to be some digging around the guns and perhaps forward on the slopes where those guns were, but, no, I did not observe much digging in front line position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your military experience, did it seem to you that the guns from the way they were positioned were in relatively stable positions or were the guns, based on their position, would they have been easily and readily moved to other locations?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge and from reporting, there was very little movement of guns. To my mind, they were all stationary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What would be the military advantage of having stationary guns in the context of a situation like Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: In a siege situation, you have guns in one location, you would be able to register as many targets as you liked. You would be able to have extreme accuracy of firing of those weapons. You would be able to respond very quickly to firing on any target that had been pre-registered and, of course, they had been there for a long time and therefore, targets, many targets, could have been pre-registered with a great deal of accuracy. That would have been the advantage of having static locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on the reports that you received from the various Papa observation posts within the city, can you make generalisations about incoming artillery and mortar fire as it related to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I would have -- the fire, to me, that was not front line fire but that that was falling within the city, appeared to me to be intentionally targeted. These are the reports that I got, that they were intentionally targeted. And I would have thought that every crossroad, every likely place of people gathering, like bread lines or water lines, general gathering places, hundreds of targets of that nature would have been pre-registered. To give you an example of accuracy, between the Presidency and what used to be, I think, the transport building, was a very narrow street. With a great degree of accuracy, mortar rounds -- it was just outside my Papa headquarters. With a great degree of accuracy, rounds could be dropped in there quite easily. And that is, to me, exceptionally good firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, were you present at any of the Serb artillery or mortar sites when those weapons were fired?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: No, no weapons were ever fired when I was on the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any discussions with any of the Bosnian Serb army crews manning those guns or mortar positions?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Through the interpreter at the Lukavica headquarters, the United Nations interpreter, I spoke -- I asked if I could speak to one of the gunners, one of the two gunners that was there. And basically I asked him one question: "How good a gunner are you?" His response was: "We could hit a cigarette packet in the middle of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I am about to go into a rather large area and I am wondering perhaps if I could seek to take the break at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps this is a good idea. We will adjourn until 5 minutes t 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that a copy has been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought my microphone was on. May I take it that a copy of the provisional translation has been provided and another copy to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Mundis

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, you alluded to earlier this morning to the shelling of Papa 5?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did that OP come under fire, mortar or artillery fire, on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, it did. There were many occasions when that OP came under mortar, artillery, and tank fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the attacks on Papa 5 commenced after your arrival in Sarajevo or was that an item that Lieutenant-Colonel Mole had handed over to you as part of his outgoing brief?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I don't think it was specific but I knew on Colonel Mole that there had been problems with all OPs and, in particular, Papa 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when, as part of your duties, you raised the issue of Papa 5 and the attacks on that OP with anyone from the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I had cause to evacuate Papa 5. I think in the last week of January, I wrote to General Galic, whom I understood to be the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, at the shelling of that OP, but it wasn't until the 13th and 14th of February, 1993, that I got particularly concerned that I may have to close that OP down because of the shelling it was receiving. And I regarded that that shelling was not indiscriminate, that it was deliberate targeted fire onto United Nations observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Artillery fire, the way it fell on the ground, and from my military experience, it was not harassing fire or indiscriminate fire. It was fired by more than one gun and the rounds from landing on the ground in an impact area, that such would indicate that it was a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the last week of January you wrote to General Galic. Do you recall how that letter left your office? What would have been the procedure?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I always, if I was writing formal letters, I wanted to make sure that it got to the people whom it was intended to receive it. Copies of that letter would -- were interpreted into the Serbian language, and copies of the English and interpreted letter would have gone to, or did go to, the Serbian LO in the PTT. There was a daily APC run into Lukavica headquarters and my UNMOs were in almost every day. The UNMOs would have taken the letter back. So I had three different channels of making sure that formal letters got to where they intended. Normally, I would follow up the day or a couple of days after by visiting that headquarters to ensure that the person whom the letter was written to had indeed received it. And I did that on every letter that I sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you first in reference to the letter that you sent the end of January 1993. Do you recall having any follow-up discussions with respect to that letter and, if so, to whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I spoke to Colonel Marcetic at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what day or date you had that discussion with him?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: It would be in early February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what, if anything, Colonel Marcetic told you with respect to the letter that you sent the end of January?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I recall his response, as was his response to many of the incidents, was basically hands in the air and saying: "This is war." I acknowledged that there was a war but that United Nations installations -- to target United Nation installations was against Geneva Conventions and against the laws of war, and anything else that I would throw. He indicated, I think at that first meeting, that they suspected there was either a mortar -- a Bosnian Presidency side mortar OP or mortar position in the area of Papa 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on what Colonel Marcetic told you, did you conduct any type of investigation to determine if, in fact, there was ABiH mortar locations near Papa 5?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I conducted that investigations with Papa 5, and they had no knowledge of a mortar line or a mortar OP in that area. I then took the investigation further and spoke to the commander of the 1 Bosnian Corps in Sarajevo, Gospodin Hajrulahovic, about that particular problem. I said to him that Papa 5 was receiving a lot of fire from time to time, that it was suspected that they may have had mortars or a mortar OP in that area, and if so, that would be using Papa 5 as a stream to do so and would he please investigate it. His response was, he would talk to his unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if Papa 5 ever reported outgoing mortar fire from their general vicinity?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: As I took a great deal of interest in Papa 5, I would have recalled that, but I do not recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned that in mid-February you followed up on your letter of the end of January. Do you recall the approximate dates that you conducted this follow-up?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the follow-up was a result of very heavy shelling on the 13th of February. Approximately 60 rounds of 122-millimetre artillery landed in close proximity to Papa 5. Some shells landed within 2 to 3 metres of the building. I had received earlier a number of armour-plated International GMCs. Unfortunately, two of those were parked in the area and they received considerable shrapnel damage. If I recall rightly, one could not be moved. Tires were burst, shrapnel on the body of the vehicle, and to our surprise, shrapnel had gone through a thin panel on the back which was not armour plated and lodged in the back seat -- or the front seat, had gone right through the back and lodged in the front seat of the vehicle. So there was some considerable damage. Fortunately, there were no UNMO casualties on the 13th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask, with the assistance of the usher, that the witness be shown P798. This document, Mr. President, is not covered by Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, I'd ask you to take a look at P798 which has now been placed before you. Is this, in fact, the letter that you sent to General Galic on 13 February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: That is the letter, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the first two sentences of this letter, and I would ask you if that refreshes your memory with respect to previous complaints that you had made with respect to shelling of Papa 5.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be now shown P797.1, again a document which is not covered by Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have P797.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That, I believe, is the B/C/S version of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, I draw your attention to P797.1. Is this the letter that you sent on 14 February, 1993, reiterating your complaints and concerns about shelling of Papa 5?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And particularly evident on page 2 is the capital letters. It doesn't have the UNPROFOR symbol on it. And would have gone out with an UNPROFOR symbol on top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the second page of the document, the sentence that is in all capital letters. What were you referring to with respect to that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I was watching the -- I observed the shelling of Papa 5 on that particular day. I had basically had enough. I was quite angry. I had been given assurances by Colonel Marcetic on more than one occasion that he knew the detailed locations of our -- of Papa 5 in particular and, indeed, all our OPs. And it just got a little bit too much to gain that they were shelling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if Colonel Marcetic -- excuse me, Colonel Marcetic ever intimated to you that you would receive a response to these three letters concerning Papa 5?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Most certainly. And I followed that up on several occasions when I visited. He told me that the matter would be investigated, that the corps commander considered it serious and that we, he used the word "we," would investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know to whom he was referring to when he said the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I would have assumed General Galic, whom the letter was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Marcetic specifically tell you that you would receive the results of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I had, first of all, asked on a previous letter, but by the time I wrote this one on the 14th, I was demanding an immediate investigation and a response by midday on the 15th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, receive a response from General Galic concerning the incidents at Papa 5?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: The only responses I ever got was: "It is still being investigated." Other than that, I have never, ever received a formal reply, written reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the complaints that you lodged with respect to Papa 5, did you on any other occasion lodge any type of complaint or protest with Colonel Marcetic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Written complaints, there may have been one or two. I cannot recall if I signed the document complaining about the theft of UNMO flack jackets and jerry cans from what we called Lima X-ray, another location on the Serb side. But I certainly verbally followed up with Colonel Marcetic about that incident. Later on, I heard from my subsector commander in the Lukavica headquarters that in fact Colonel Marcetic had told them that they believed they had found the soldiers responsible for having held UNMOs at gunpoint whilst they took these flack jackets and two jerry cans of fuel. I was reasonably happy. And I think the flack jackets were returned, and we obviously didn't worry too much about the fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to any complaints or protests that you made or may have made to Colonel Marcetic with respect to shelling or sniping of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Every time I did get to speak to Colonel Marcetic, I raised several issues every time. The sniping of UNMO was obviously my great concern, that I wouldn't get any UNMOs wounded or killed, the firing on Kosevo hospital, the shelling, what appeared to be harassing shelling, of Sarajevo that killed civilians. I even got to the stage where I had some rapport with Colonel Marcetic, I felt that as professional military officers. I actually told him that I did not mind in particular if he was shelling the front line positions but I could not accept under any circumstances the shelling into the city that killed civilians and shelling hospitals. Those were the major, major things I complained about every time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was Colonel Marcetic's response when you told him this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: His initial response was always hands up like this and telling me: "This is war." The interpreter would also say that perhaps Colonel Marcetic thought that I didn't understand what was going on. And that is about the sum total of that, except for a meeting later in my piece where, if you wanted me to talk about, I could, he went a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe that for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: That was a meeting I had with Colonel Marcetic that I didn't expect to have. I happened to be in the Lima headquarters with my UNMOs, and the liaison officer at the headquarters said that Colonel Marcetic wanted to see me and that he would come down to the UNMO headquarters, which is perhaps a little bit unusual that he didn't ask me to go to his office. For some reason, I was in a mood where I would not sit down and listen to any excuses. Something had upset me. And I launched into Colonel Marcetic about everything that I have covered with him in the previous two months. I recall the meeting very well. He came into the little UNMO room. As I told you before, it was a rather cramped room. There were about three UNMOs, myself, and Colonel Marcetic in the room. We offered him a cup of coffee, which he accepted, coffee or tea, and I launched into him about all the incidents and again reiterated that I considered him a war criminal because of the shelling and killing of civilians in Sarajevo. I covered all the other incidents about deliberate shelling of our observation posts, firing on hospitals, the cheating and lying that I had received since I had been there. And I have to say that was on both sides. And it was only then that I ever saw him perhaps have some remorse because he -- he said through the interpreter who had interpreted -- the interpreter had told me that he fully understood what I was talking about, and his words were to the effect: "I am sorry all this is going on. This is war." He put his head in his hands, and that basically concluded the meeting. I interpreted from that that there was no denial that all these things were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber any instance when you lodged a complaint or protest with Major Indjic, what his response was?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I had quite a lot to do with Major Indjic. Are you talking about the Major Indjic at the PTT?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I am talking about the person that you have described to the change as Major Indjic.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Okay, Major Indjic was the Serb LO at the PTT. I had many dealings with him in general about "tell Lukavica to shop shelling," about one incident in particular whilst the shelling on the 14th of February 1993 of the Papa 5 headquarters. It was under what I would call intense shelling. I was observing it. I went into the OPs room and Lima 7 on the eastern flank of Sarajevo that had that good overview of batteries on the eastern flank, basically come up with a perfect fire mission. They were describing a fire mission. If I recall rightly, there was no firing going on in Sarajevo at that particular time. Lima 7 reported a battery on the eastern side firing. They even went to the point of saying on their radio: "Shot over," which meant in military terms that they had gone ahead and fired, and they reported several shots. My -- at the same time, Papa 6 OP, which was almost in direct line of sight of any rounds coming from that battery towards Papa 5, warned us out that there were rounds going past the front of their position. It became evident that those rounds were landing in and around or around Papa 5. This all occurred in a very short space of time. We even got to the point of "shot over" Lima -- from Lima 7. Papa 6 would say, "We can hear it." And we saw the splashes, which is the term for explosions, at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the far end. We even had a time of flight. One officer actually timed the shells. I can't exactly recall but it was somewhere in the vicinity of 15 to 17 seconds. There was no doubt in my mind that the battery that was firing on the eastern flank of Sarajevo was targeting Papa 5. As I said, this all occurred in a very short space of time. I raced down four flights of stairs to Major Indjic's office. This is the incident where I forgot to turn the door handle, kicked the door and all the glass fell out. They -- Major Indjic was rather surprised that I was there in that mood, and I demanded in no uncertain terms to stop shelling Papa 5 and that I wanted an immediate ceasefire. He immediately got on a telephone and told me that he had spoken to his headquarters, that they would cease firing, and we had 30 minutes to evacuate the OP. I was arranging at that stage - this was all concurrent - the French APC supporting the UNMOs, to get standby to go and evacuate that OP. They were actually on the move fairly quickly. The firing ceased. We evacuated the OP. Just as they were leaving the OP, the OP once again come under fire. And I remember it like as if it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific incidents where you raised complaints or protests with Major Indjic about shelling or sniping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: No. I don't have a recall of me personally doing that. But I know that Major Keith Carswell and the DSMO before me did so, had liaison with Major Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the liaison officer at Lukavica barracks. Do you recall whether you had any discussions with him concerning targeting of civilians by either artillery mortar or sniping fire?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I personally didn't have a lot to do with him. A similar situation is perhaps that General Galic had with me in that I preferred to deal with somebody of more senior rank. However, there was one incident that I remember quite well. It must have been prior to 21, 26th February, because I was at that stage on leave. Captain Pat Henneberry was the subunit commander there. So I would guess it was about -- about the time that Papa 5 was shelled, so mid-February 1993. I had previously put Captain Pat Henneberry in charge of the Lima UNMOs after Commandant Beary had left. It was my choice. I considered Captain Pat Henneberry to have an extremely professional approach to the task of the UNMOs and I was very happy with his performance. I tried to get to know the UNMOs, to see how they were reacting to the situation. It was not easy. And on this particular afternoon, I was sitting in the UNMO headquarters, and he seemed to be very upset about something. Whether I asked him if he was upset, I don't recall, but he did tell me that the Serb liaison officer -- why he was pretty upset was that the Serb liaison officer had told him that the shelling into Sarajevo and the killing of civilians was deliberate. I interpreted that to mean that it was an intentional part of the corps plan of the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did this statement by Captain Henneberry surprise you at all?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: It surprised me from the point of view that here was a young captain trying to do his job and he felt so sad knowing that children and civilians -- innocent civilians were being killed. It surprised me that he wasn't aware of it, that he may have assumed that that was the case. But here he had direct proof, if you like. It may not have been the truth, of course, but he was very upset about it. To me, it was very evident that that had been going on. It wasn't earth-shattering news to me at all because I had come to the conclusion that harassing morale-lowering fire was a fait accompli in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
