utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, were you aware of any rumours to the effect that forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were shelling the civilian population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite strong rumours that that was the case, that they were either rogue forces or somebody who was sniping within Sarajevo, that is, Bosnians sniping on Bosnians, and that Bosnians had shelled themselves, if you like, within the city. It was quite strong rumours floating around to that effect. There was never, to my knowledge, any proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you, through the UNMO reporting chain, ever have any evidence that that was the case, for example, a Papa position reporting outgoing mortar fire followed a few seconds later by another Papa position reporting incoming mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: No. I cannot recall -- I cannot recall anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During your tenure, you have no evidence that came to your attention that the Bosnians were targeting other Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: The only evidence, not first-hand and not through my chain, it was reported through the sector, was that several mortar rounds that landed next to a French OP on the entry to the Sarajevo airport. By crater analysis, it was concluded that the rounds could only have come from a Bosnian position. I am not an expert on crater analysis, but I understand the work that they do, and they were reasonably happy that it had come from Bosnian fire. The only other two incidents that I recall, and I do not know if it was proven as a result of investigations, was the day or the days that Vance and Dole visited Sarajevo and the day when Boutros Boutros-Ghali visited Sarajevo when I was there. It just so happened that as their convey was approaching the area of the Presidency, mortar rounds landed on the road in front of them, as I understand it, not a lot, but mortar rounds landed. It was strongly suspected that those rounds came from Bosnian forces and not Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you understand that an investigation was in fact carried out concerning the incidents involving Vance, Dole and Boutros Boutros-Ghali?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I do not know the results of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other that those three incidents, that is, the French forces at the airport, the Vance Dole convoy and the Butros Butros-Ghali convoy, are you aware of any other investigations that were conducted by any organisation concerning attacks by Bosnian forces on Bosnian civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that other incidents were investigated, sniping and shelling, that may have been suspected to have come from Bosnian forces. But I do not recall the exact details, nor do I recall the outcomes of those investigations. There were many, many reports that went to General Morillon from a whole range of people, including UNHCR that were out in the community, but I am not aware of any conclusive results in relation to Bosnians shelling Bosnians other than the ones I have told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience and the reporting up the chain of command to you from the various UNMOs, what conclusions did you draw about the source or sources of the artillery and mortar fire that were incoming to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Into the city itself as opposed to front lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I had previously, this morning, have told you that I have no doubt whatsoever, given my knowledge of the use of artillery and mortars, that there is no way that it was other than harassing deliberate morale-lowering fire intentionally targeted into the city of Sarajevo and not on to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the source of that fire?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: On many occasions, Sarajevo was quiet. There was no outgoing fire. I could only assume that the noise was made by firing from Bosnian Serb gun positions. And on many days, UNMOs would report firing as outgoing from a particular location and rounds would be falling into the city. Whilst one can -- may never be exactly sure that the rounds that were outgoing were the ones falling in the city, having watched this go on for some time, my conclusion was quite clear as to who was -- that the Bosnian Serb were firing into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, were you aware of incidents where individuals attempting to cross the airport were the victim of sniping attacks?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: The French Foreign Legion based at the airport were responsible for the airport area, its security, and all incidents around there. Therefore, reporting up to me was not -- I was not directly involved in that particular area. However, from sector commander conferences, the French CO every morning would give a report of crossings, attempted crossings, of the Sarajevo airport during the previous night. I was quite amazed at the number of people who would be going in either directions across that airport, and I think it was very, very difficult task that the French Foreign Legion had at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on these briefings, did you receive any information concerning casualties of individuals attempting to cross the airport?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. Normally at that morning briefing, the commanding officer would report the number of people attempting to cross the airfield and the number of casualties that had been received that night, that is casualties being fired upon from other than UN forces. I don't think that the French fired a shot. Now, who caused the casualties, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection concerning, first of all, the numbers of people cross the airport?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I recall from sit-reps that I would write at nighttime from the morning conference information I received figures like 200. 300 would be -- 300 would be a fairly heavy night. And numbers like 90, 101, I think I recall in one incident. So it was between 80 and up to 300. It seemed to get more and more as my time there went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the number of people that were reported as either wounded or killed as an attempt to cross the airport?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Some nights, surprisingly, there were none. Other nights, I think it was in the very small -- I recall the figure 2, 5. I don't recall -- I do not recall any more than 5. It may well have been but they were very small figures, mainly from -- in fact only, if I recall rightly, from sniper fire or from small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident in which you reported in a situation report: "sniping against a bus full of civilians, Polish civilians."

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. That was a report given to me in which the UNMO involved I think was another New Zealander, Major Howard Duffy. A bus load of Polish civilians was moving between Sarajevo proper and the airport, going down to the airport road. That bus load of civilians was fired upon. It would have been approximately adjacent to the suburb and the pocket called Nedzarici. If I understand correctly, there were several killed, Polish civilians killed in that incident, and several wounded. The UNMOs were travelling or had caught up to the busses that had stopped on the side of the road when they were fired upon. They were being escorted by French APCs. It was described to me as a bit of a shambles. The UNMOs, if I recall correctly, always carried shell dressings, moved forward on the right-hand side down a little dip and started to administer first aid to two of the victims. At the same time, the reports said that the French APC had called back to the OPs room in Sarajevo at the PTT for ambulances, and I think the UNMOs did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, you have testified about the theft of flack jackets and jerry cans. Were you also aware of incidents in which Motorola radios owned by the United Nations were stolen or pilfered?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. During my time there, I think I would have recalled at least 4, 5 occasions on the Serb side and I think about three occasions on the Presidency side, that Motorolas had been stolen or taken at gunpoint and that we had no doubt whatsoever that our communications were being monitored by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you ever recall instances in which non-UN personnel were using the UN frequencies on the Motorola radios?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbo-Croat language was used on the Motorolas, not that frequently, but we certainly heard that language going across the Motorolas. Indeed, I recall it was common practice on leaving Sarajevo for the call sign leaving - my call sign happened to be uniform 9 - that they would just ring up and say: "Everybody, this is uniform," whatever - in my case, uniform 9 - "leaving Sarajevo for the last time." And I recall when I was going to the airport that I was farewelled by several UNMOs receiving my call and also the Serb-Croat language was heard, and I assume it was a farewell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P809 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, I would ask you to take a look at P809. On the face of this document, was it created by the UNPROFOR Lima headquarters at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, the Lima headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And based on the date indicated on the face of this document, was that during the time when you were the senior military observer?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, 15th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like you to look at the group of the first six names on this document listed under commanders, Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which of those six named individuals you encountered during the time you were in Sarajevo? And "encountered," I mean met briefly or met with or knew or were aware of.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Well, certainly General Galic, and certainly the man that I did most work with, Colonel Marcetic, second named. The other four names do not ring any bells, although I notice there is a person they call Colonel Zarkovic, whom I would have thought that he was the group -- it looks like it says, "In charge of the group for cooperation of UNPROFOR." I would have put a "J" instead of the "Z." But whether or not that is the same person, I do not recall. I understood his name -- I understood that person's name to be Jakavic with a "J" and not Zarkovic. I do not recall any of those other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That document can be retrieved from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, do you recall attending a Serbian Christmas function in Pale during the time you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I found the fact that I was attending a bit rather unusual. General Morillon had passed a message to the sector commander Colonel Razek that he had been invited to attend the Serbian Christmas dinner the 7th of January in Pale. The General Morillon did not think it appropriate to go, but that the senior military observer, having the umbrella of neutrality, he saw no problem in me attending and I was basically told to attend. I took the opportunity to visit Mokro barracks to the north-east of Sarajevo during that visit. We left early. I took an interpreter from the Serbian Corps headquarters. Her name was Jadranka. Jadranka. And I think my driver escort for the day was another New Zealander, Captain Petar Flint. We visited the UNMOs at Lima 7 and I think it was about midday-ish that we went to a location that was like a community hall in Pale where there was a Christmas dinner. And I attended that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were any senior military officers from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps present at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I do not recall anybody from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps but there were some rather senior officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, who was the most senior military officer present at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: General Mladic. There was General Gvero, and there was the President of Bosnia, Bosnian Serb Republic, Dr. Karadzic, and there was also Dr. Lukic, whom I understood to be the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the course of that dinner, did you have the opportunity to have any discussions with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: It was not a particularly long dinner, and I appreciated that. There was not a lot of alcohol there either, which I appreciated. The initial discussions through interpretation with General Mladic were that he reminded me that New Zealand troops had been through Yugoslavia many years ago. He invited me to establish, or he would have no difficulty with me to establish an UNMO presence at his Pale headquarters, which later on was, in fact, established. He indicated that he had no intentions of pulling his guns away from surrounding Sarajevo. He indicated that the only way for peace was to form a buffer between the city and the surrounding countryside, which would have taken brigades and brigades of United Nations military personnel. Those were the initial conversations, although I didn't speak to him that long. He set me back on my heels a little bit when I -- towards the end of the dinner, I asked him through interpretation: "Where is all this going to end?" And his response was - it shocked me a little bit - that Muslims were not real people, that as long as he remained the commander of the Bosnian Serb army, he would kill all Muslims or push them into the sea, and I did not have a response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Similarly, did you subsequently have a discussion with President Izetbegovic concerning his views as to how the conflict could come to an end?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: Not with President Izetbegovic. I only met him a couple of times very briefly. No, I discussed it with the supreme commander of the Bosnian army, whose name was Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did General Halilovic tell you in response to the question: "How would the war end?"

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER
utterances.text: I am not too sure he was a general. Certainly, he was introduced to me as "Gospodin." I think it was accepted that he was a general. He spoke about the history of Muslims in particular in and around Sarajevo and that he considered they had a right to be there ever since the Ottoman Empire, and that he would fight with every man, woman and child to save what was rightfully theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Cutler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Colonel Cutler, for procedural reasons, the order as far as your examination is concerned is that cross-examination will not start right away but you will be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence next Monday. I couldn't give you an exact time because it depends on the developments from now until Monday morning, whether we could start right away on Monday or that it would be later that day. When I say "Monday morning," I have to correct myself, because we are sitting Monday in the afternoon, so that would mean that, as I hope, somewhere in the afternoon next Monday you will be cross-examined by the Defence. I hope at least that you are still available, and that you could stay in The Hague until next Monday. I was informed that you had been stuck already for quite a few days here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am at the Court's pleasure in this regard. I have informed my people back in New Zealand that I may have to stay on a little longer. They are happy with that, and I am getting to know The Hague quite well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you will be excused for this moment, but we expect you back next Monday, and I think if you would leave in one way or the other a place where you can be reached so that we could inform you whether we expect you to be cross-examined right in the beginning of the afternoon session, that is at quarter past 2.00, or let's say one hour later or two hours later. May I meanwhile instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony given until now in this Court. That means also not with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you are excused for this very moment. And would you please, Mr. Usher, escort Colonel Cutler out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Mundis or Mr. Ierace, or Mr. Waespi. I don't know who to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Gardemeister, who will be taken by Mr. Waespi. I might indicate that we are hopeful that we can finish his testimony entirely in the time left today. Perhaps we will see how long the examination-in-chief takes. I expect it will be very quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The usher has gone. Mr. Mundis, you are standing. You are asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I may be excused, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on one condition, that if you meet the usher out of this courtroom that you will frankly ask him to bring in Mr. Gardemeister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Waespi. On my clock it is already the afternoon, but only since two minutes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps it is a good moment to indicate that we will only discuss two exhibits with this witness out of the ones we have indicated to the Defence. So perhaps if these could be prepared for the sake of quickness, perhaps, and those will be Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 1448. That is a document dated 22nd July, 1993. And the second document will be Prosecution Exhibit 1579, and this is dated 26th -- 28th August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gardemeister Kukkola, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You speak English so I don't have to ask you if you hear me in a language you understand. Is English your native language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not. My native language is Finnish and Swedish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finnish and Swedish. If there ever would be a problem in expressing yourself in English, please indicate so because we would like to prevent whatever kind of confusion in this courtroom caused by language problems. Mr. Gardemeister Kukkola, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth at the beginning of your testimony. The text of the declaration is handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. .JUDGE ORIE: Now, the next pages are not necessary. Please be seated, Mr. Gardemeister. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps if the usher could again assist the case manager. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gardemeister Kukkola.

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please, for the record, state your name?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Jorma Gardemeister, formerly Kukkola.

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: I was born in Helsinki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you serve since 1969 in the Finnish army?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And as part of that, or perhaps besides that, were you serving in the United Nations and various -- on various occasions among others in countries such as Cyprus and Lebanon?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You were posted to the former Yugoslavia as an UNMO effective from 11th May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And between 11th June, 1993 and 19th October, 1993, were you the SMO, the senior military observer, for the Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As part of your duties, did you meet with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many times would that occur?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: During my four and a half months in Sarajevo, I think I met him around four times, four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also meet with senior subordinates of General Galic and can you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, I met Mr. -- Colonel Milosevic and Colonel Milovanovic, and I also met, of course, the liaison officers in Lukavica several times, and several commanders on the Serbian side of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gardemeister. As a result of these meetings with General Galic and his subordinates and also based on information you had from your UNMOs, did you form an impression as to the degree of command and control of General Galic the way he exercised it over his troops?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a chance to meet General Galic for long meetings. What I -- what I heard from my UNMOs, and especially the team leader in Lukavica, it was rather confirmed that General Galic had a good command of his Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gardemeister, I would like to raise with you one particular incident and I would like you to be shown a document, and it is again a document under seal, number Prosecution number 1448, dated the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I am wondering, Your Honours, because he will talk about this document, whether it would be appropriate to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if the content of the document will be discussed and since the content of the document is protected, we could turn into closed session. I am just wondering whether private session would be enough as well. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps he would like to place it onto the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course we would have to -- if it is put on the ELMO, although as far as I can see now, it is just text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It is. You can certainly read it out so we can stay in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber always prefers to have the -- to have as little as possible infringement on the principle of the public character of the trial and, therefore, being no pictures there, I think that private session would do. And I see, Madam Registrar, agrees that from a technical point of view that this would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then turn into private session at this moment. Mr. Waespi, would you please assist me in indicating when it is not necessary any more to remain any more in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that "PS" has disappeared so we are in open session again. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have, Mr. Gardemeister, occasion to meet a number of commanders of artillery units on the Bosnian Serb side apart from the meeting you just described?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes. During my four and a half times -- four and a half months stay in Sarajevo, I did visit most of the Bosnian Serb artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion about the professionalism of the officers and the crews, the soldiers, you have seen?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was rather surprised of the good professionalism of the artillery officers. We had long sessions and talked about how they are manoeuvreing with their devices and artillery, mortars, and so on. And the impression was very professional, they gave to me. I didn't speak to all the gun soldiers or privates, but the overall impression was professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also form an opinion as to the accuracy of gunfire, artillery fire, perhaps mortar, based on conversations you had with commanders on the site?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: I can give you the one example. When I was visiting the artillery position east of Sarajevo, up on the high mountain, and I talk to the artillery commander and I ask him to point out the objects in Sarajevo itself, and he gave me a short briefing. Then I ask him that, "What about UNMO stations? Are you aware where the UNMO stations are situated within Sarajevo?" He pointed out immediately and said that, "You can relax because I know exactly where your positions are and our aim is rather accurate."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he tell you further anything about the degree of accuracy he and his troops were able to achieve?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, I was told by him that they can hit specifically with artillery in a very, very small goal or aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he indicate what type of goal or aim that could be? Did he give an example for that?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Just pointing out some big houses but we didn't go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gardemeister, I would like to show you a second and, indeed, the last document and this is Prosecution Exhibit 1579. It is again, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could have the same procedure again, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find confirmation that we are again in open session. You will now be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence, Mr. Gardemeister. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gardemeister, good day. Your mandate in Sarajevo was from the 11th of June, 1993 up until the 19th of October, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that while you had your mandate in Sarajevo during that period, in reaction to the events that took place at that time, 27th of May, 1993, you gave a statement to the investigators for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: 27th of May I -- I was not in Sarajevo then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am asking whether with regard to your stay in Sarajevo during the 1999 -- 1993 period, did you give the investigators of the Prosecution on the 27th and 28th of May, 1998 a -- a statement about this?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: My former stay in Sarajevo, yes, I did, for the Finnish authorities. And also later on, to Mr. Cleaver, who came back on the way to Finland to interview me, and I gave him statement to him also regarding my experiences while I was in Sarajevo if that is the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when you gave your statement you said that you were present as a member of the team of observers of the UN observers and that you were present at observation posts in Sarajevo. Were those observation posts Lima and Papa?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes. I was the SMO senior military observer responsible for Lima and Papa teams in my office in the famous PTT building inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that your office was in the PTT building in Sarajevo, during your stay there, did you have any information that in the area of the building that you used, was the building a military target? Were there mobile mortars which were -- by the PTT building and which were used by members of the 1st Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that, couple of cases like that, when the Bosnian Corps brought mortars in the vicinity on a tractor or tractors, but I don't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Sarajevo during that period, how often did members of the 1st Corps of the BH army use the PTT building in this manner as a place from which they would fire mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: I remember, as I told you, one or two cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you also stated that, when you were describing your job, that you took a count of combat activities and of the amassing of the army, or rather that you would report on combat activities such as the amassing of men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I have to read it once again. Our main task was to report on military actions in Sarajevo area, and it consisted of counting of outgoing shells and counting of incoming shells. Also, we were supporting the warring factions when it came to the force to reach a ceasefire. Those were our main tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you had to support the warring parties, can you tell us with regard to the period for which you had the mandate, do you have any information as to whether in the area of the town of Sarajevo and beyond, there was any fighting between the two parties in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to fightings between the two parties, during my time, there was lot of fighting, exchange of fire going on, on separate, let's say, time limits. Or sometimes we had extensive fire. Sometimes the situation was a little bit more stable, with only sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement which you gave to the investigators, on page 4 of your statement, you said that you helped with the repairs of utilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: That is correct. We had one or two military observers with a main task of supporting the -- that task in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you helped with repairing the utilities, can you tell us whether during that period you had any information about how the public utilities were damaged? What was the cause of the damage to the utilities?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: I am not aware of the details because actually, when I took over, they were about to finish with that kind of missions with UNMOs. But I understand that they were concerned with repairs of electricity and other utilities inside Sarajevo. And the UNMOs would accompany the technicians and were also to provide the communications, and in case of problems, to support the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about when they were trying to solve the problems relating to the utilities, was a mixed war commission responsible for this? Did it have any authority in this area? And when I say a "mixed war commission," did it consist of representatives of the warring factors both from the Muslim and the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: I do not know. I was not -- I didn't have that detailed information about the mission. As I told you, that works were almost completed when I took over.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, for the period of June and July in the area of the Sarajevo battlefield, were you aware of the fact that there was combat operation which was being conducted and which was called "Lukavica 1993"?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: No, that -- that code name, I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at the time of your mandate an agreement was reached according to which the Serbian forces should leave the area between Igman and the Ilidza and that they should hand this area over to the control of UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that and I was very much dealing with this mission from UNMO side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you had much to do with that task, that you were very involved in this task, do you know whether forces of the BH army --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you were asked to repeat the question, but you might not have heard it. It was on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear that. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, and do you know whether, ignoring the agreements of UNPROFOR with the Serbian side, was the area of Igman left to the units of the BH army with UNPROFOR's agreement? Was this area handed over to units of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, what happened on Igman didn't really go as planned. When Bosnian Serb forces were withdrawn, or withdraw according to the plan, the French UNPROFOR did not immediately get deployed, but what really happened was in some states that ABiH, the 1st Corps, took over instead of the French unit. So there was not -- the planning was not come to practice as it was planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, on page 8 of your statement, and I am going to quote part of it, part of your statement. It is page 8 and it is the third paragraph, you said: "The military targets in the town included the Presidency, the corps command post and the Igman road." On the basis of what you stated there, can you explain to us how the units of the 1st Corps were deployed of the BH army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Generally speaking or in one particular area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said -- when you spoke about the military targets, I said that you said the staff command and command posts. Could you tell us about the command post of the brigade? How many brigades were there in fact in Sarajevo which belonged to the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: The 1st Corps, the Bosnian 1st Corps, comprises of ten brigades, one of the brigades being an HVO brigade. That was the situation within Sarajevo itself during my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you gave us a list of these military targets which I have read out from your statement, could you be so kind as to mention certain other elements of the combat and operative order of the units of the 1st Corps of the BH army and which represent legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, which were legitimate targets, of course, when it comes to the command posts, the HQ of 1st Corps was located in downtown Sarajevo itself and the brigade command posts were in the respective AORs in Sarajevo. And later on the 1st Corps had unit, of course, up on the Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your mandate, while you had a mandate, did you visit the command posts of the brigades or any other command posts which belonged to the 1st Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: During my stay, I did visit 1st Corps HQ around five, six times. I did visit only one of the -- of the brigades HQ in Sarajevo itself. Furthermore, I did visit several times the 1st Corps command post up on the Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that within the 1st Corps of the BH army that there were 10 brigades, could you tell us whether you know how many military targets there are, legitimate military targets, there were in Sarajevo, what the total number was, if we consider the fact that within the framework of the 1st Corps, the part of the town that was under the 1st Corps, there were ten brigades?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Then it would come to a total of 11 military targets when it comes to the command posts, and groups is another thing. Of course, they were also military targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that the logistics basis of the firing positions of the artillery and mortars, the positions of battalions, companies and platoons, observation posts of the commanders of companies and of platoons and then special battalions, are these elements which consist -- compose a brigade and, in your opinion, are these also military targets?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Of course, but when it comes to Sarajevo, the situation was not that -- that simple. I mean, the brigades were not as sites of normal brigades and it was not very clear where you had military target as one has normally when it comes to, let's say, a normal European unit. The battalions were not as -- having as many soldiers as a normal European battalion normally includes. So the thing, where were the targets is, it cannot be that easily described.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say this, would you agree with me that it was very difficult to tell military targets from civilian facilities in a situation when military targets were positioned in an urban part of town which is used by civilians?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Partly yes, but it is my -- as I understand, the most of the military concentration of those 10 brigades were concentrated near so-called confrontation line and not in where the most of civilian people lived in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say this, do you confirm that you know the position of the brigades of the 1st Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes, we had -- we had a kind of sketch and our UNMO Papa team was rather well aware where this 10 brigades had a concentration within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your statement that it was from Lima positions that brigades of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps were observed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us from one Lima position, how many brigades were you able to observe?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Normally, one Lima position, we were covering one brigade. And sometimes two Lima positions were covering part of the same brigade. At the main plan how we did deploy our Lima teams was also related to the artillery positions of BSA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, at the time when you -- during your mandate, how many Lima positions were on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, when we started, when I took over in Sarajevo, we had actually situation where we had a kind of -- kind of a command of Lima in Lukavica and 11 stations around Sarajevo. But when I left -- before I left Sarajevo, I did flatten the Lima stations so that only, if I remember right, six or seven were left, and a substation commander in Lukavica was, let's say, downsized to a team leader and the teams which I am referring to in Lima side were from that moment on only stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, how many Papa positions were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo, we had -- we had only three Papa positions within Sarajevo, inside Sarajevo, and one Papa position in Hrasnica at the foot of Igman. When the situation became more tense, I established one more Papa station, Papa 4, close to Zuc area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In a situation in one part of town, you had 10 brigades. Would you assess that four observation posts were sufficient to inform about the activities of the 1st Corps, i.e. of those 10 brigades?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, if ABiH army had artillery and more heavier weapons as it did have, I would say that, no, it is not enough. It was not enough. But in the case when they were mostly armed only by weapons like rifles and some mortars, I would say that, since we knew where their positions were and this so-called heavy arms, in my opinion, it was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I put it to you that the army of BH had five tanks, that it also had rocket launchers, Howitzers, would you agree with me that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: What we did confirm was that they had two tanks, no artillery, only mortars and small arms. Rocket launchers, I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 8 of your statement, you said: "When it was just shelling between the two armies, we did not really protest the shelling. When the shelling was only military against military, we did not really protest the shelling." My question, when you said this, how did you know that this was an exchange of fire in an area of the front line or -- and that it was not shelling of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, through our UNMO stations, I got the fax to my office, and the decision or conclusion was made in most of the cases in a good cooperation with UNPROFOR French units and the UNPROFOR HQ in the same building were I had my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you got the facts and data, could you tell us in which way would you get these?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Normally, when it comes to -- came to exchange of fire, normally, the first source of information and the one I most relied on was my UNMO stations inside Sarajevo and outside Sarajevo. And also I got information from -- from the French battalions, liaison officers from both sides, Bosniak and also from the liaison officers from Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. When you received such information, my question was: How did you get it? Was it in a written form or was it over the phone?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Normally, it was over the phone or on VHF radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you received a piece of information over the phone, did you check that information that you received?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Normally, always we did check the information and that was done either by our UNMO teams, I sent UNMO teams to the spot, and also what I did normally, I got in touch with the French units, and so it was always a kind of double-check in question, if it was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, looking at the clock, keeping in mind that there might be a need for re-examination of the witness and there might be some questions as well from the Bench, I am taking into account that you used your time similar, or even more, than examination-in-chief. Could you please conclude? If there are one or two remaining questions, of course, that is no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have another couple.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, under page 8 of your statement, you said "the greatest danger for the Bosnian Serb civilians was the sniping activity and that was also the greatest danger for the soldiers on the front line. Chief of Staff of the Vogosca brigade said that his soldiers suffered more from sniper activities than from anything else." Could you confirm whether this is correct?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: What the Chief of Staff of Vogosca brigade told me on Zuc when I was visiting the front line with him was confirmed by me because he told me so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you tell us from which positions and which army was firing towards Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Towards Vogosca it was -- it was ABiH 1st Corps firing towards Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: One more question: When you spoke of an incident that you investigated on the 26th of July 1993 and you said that it was established that the blame lay on the Serb side, could you tell us which mortars -- which mortars were used by the Serb army and which were the Muslim army where your observers were on the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Serbs were using 82, 120, I suppose, and also the very small one, 40 or 50. And artillery which was not -- which was not used --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How about the Muslims? Which mortars were used by Muslims? Would you agree with me that they were using exactly the same type of mortars as used by the Serbs, that is 120 and 82 millimetres and 60?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because they were ex-JNA arms. But the thing is that they did not have artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke here of a mortar incident. I am just interested to hear from you how you could assume, considering that both sides used that same type of mortars, how could you assume that the mortar was fired from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: In this particular case, the artillery craters were the precising facts, but normally it was really very difficult to say when it comes to mortar shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is the crater trace, from which weapon -- from which weapon was it?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: I don't remember any more that fact. 120 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Waespi, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has a question for you, Mr. Gardemeister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I just wanted to ask you, you said that, and I am quoting in English, [In English] "The brigade command posts were in the respective AORs in Sarajevo." What do you mean by AORs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, AOR means "area of responsibility." The Bosniak brigades in Sarajevo was divided when it comes to AOR to then brigades of ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, there were 10 areas of responsibility, as you say, of command, as you say in Sarajevo itself, in the city, and you knew the locality of these command posts?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo was split in 10 AORs of respective brigades and our UNMOs, we were aware of the command posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said also that it wasn't easy to distinguish a military target inside the city. Are you saying that the military targets were difficult to tell apart from the civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: Well, in some cases, perhaps, yes. But as I told before, the main concentrations, as far as I know, were more, let's say, related to the so-called confrontation line. But, of course there were logistics bases. I am not aware of the details inside Sarajevo town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question would refer to the officer who was punished, and I'm referring to the incident that you spoke of during the shelling that was observed from the Lima 7 position, and I believe that it was targeting the French positions. You said that, after your request, the officer in charge was punished. Could you confirm that he was punished or was this just an information that was transmitted to you without any evidence?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: First of all, we did not ask BSA to take any measures. We just told them what was the conclusion of our inquiry. And the second thing is we are not aware if that officer was punished. We were just told so and we didn't have any chance to confirm it by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Gardemeister, I have got a few questions for you as well. First you have told us about the French element of UNPROFOR that was near the stadium and which was attacked. Could you tell us, what stadium, because the Chamber by now knows that there were more stadiums in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: It was near Skanderija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a second question is about the calibres, the calibre used during that mortar attack. Your testimony was that you came to the conclusion on the basis -- well, on a series of grounds that the fire came from BSA artillery positions. And you said the first one was that the calibre used was not normally used by the 1st Corps. So you deduced something from the calibre. At a question of counsel for the Defence, you answered that apart from artillery that the same calibres were used 60, 80, to 120 and you added that you did not remember, quite well, what calibre was involved here. But at one side you tell us that the calibres used were the same, and on the other hand, you tell us that the calibres was one of the elements on which you deduced that the fire must have come from BSA positions. Could you further explain to me how you could deduce that in view of the fact that you testified that they would use the same calibres?

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: The basic thing is that this French element of UNPROFOR was shelled by mortar and artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And artillery, yes.

utterances.speaker: JORMA KALEVI GARDEMEISTER
utterances.text: And since ABiH did not use artillery in that area, and they didn't have artillery, as far as we know, and also according to our logbook, and the logbook, there was no outgoing ABiH artillery or mortar. So it was impossible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was one of the other reasons you gave us. But so it was not on the calibre of the mortars, but on the artillery part of the attack that you made your conclusions. These were my questions. This concludes, Mr. Gardemeister, your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming. It is a long way for you, as well, to The Hague. Thank you very much for coming and testifying and answering questions of both parties and of the Bench. I wish you a good trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Gardemeister out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, I think we have two documents both under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1579 under seal, UNPROFOR report; Exhibit P1448, under seal, UNPROFOR report, 26 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both documents are -- I wanted to say admitted into evidence but I only then saw that you were on your feet, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence objects to the tendering of the Exhibit 179 considering that we do not have a seal or a signature on this document regardless of the fact that the witness, during the examination-in-chief, said that this was a document which was done on the computer. Therefore, we have no information and we contest to the origin of this document and we contest its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: THE COURT: Mr. Waespi, would you like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, only briefly, Your Honours. I think the witness clearly identified that he knew what this document was all about. He could readily explain what was written in there. He explained why this form was different from the ones they used before, and I don't think there is any doubt that this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the objection against admission of this document is denied. The witness has identified the document as the document in the form and of the content as he could testify about. So the document is admitted into evidence just as the other one 1448, both under seal. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have an urgent matter to raise in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it is urgent. Of course, I need the approval of the interpreters and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I have another problem can you do this as quickly as possible, otherwise the Stakic case has to wait for more time. So we will turn into closed session and if you could just do it as brief as possible. Could we turn in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
